title: The hill before the records
place: Llandough hill, above the River Ely
rules: no narrator, no archive bookend, no fourth wall: characters speak only to each other, a child or the animals
each half sandboxed in its own period: no talk of buildings, records or events from another age
Welsh audio (nearest living language to Brittonic), en/es subtitles; Rioplatense Spanish

cast.B_JOHN: the Iron Age elder (c. 200 BC); a Romano-British farmer (c. AD 200); invented faces
cast.A_MARY: the roundhouse mother; the farmer's wife; invented faces

removed: F003 shot 5 (Gran's round house / the barn and the oxen): a character reaching across time to buildings of another age
old F002 script lines looking ahead ("somebody will build on that one day") and the Nia/Grandson archive bookend

shots.direction: Dawn, about 200 BC. A small homestead on the top of Llandough hill: thatched roundhouses with wattle-and-daub walls inside an earth bank, a raised granary on posts and a hurdle fold with a few small dark cattle. Smoke seeps up through the thatch and mist lifts off the reed marsh of the Ely far below. Caption: c. 200 BC, Llandough hill above the River Ely; spoken in modern Welsh, the nearest living language to theirs.
captions: c. 200 BC · Llandough hill, above the River Ely

shots.direction: The roundhouse mother stands in the low doorway, the hearth glowing behind her. She looks up at the smoke and speaks to her husband: the weather should hold, so they can bring the corn in today.

lines.cy: Wnaiff y tywydd ddal heddiw? Mae'r mwg yn codi'n syth. Dim gwynt, dim glaw. Fe gawn ni'r ŷd i mewn.
lines.en: Will the weather hold today? Smoke's going straight up. No wind, no rain. We'll get the corn in.
lines.es: ¿Aguantará el tiempo hoy? El humo sube derecho. Ni viento ni lluvia. Vamos a entrar el grano.

shots.direction: The elder, grey-bearded in a brown wool cloak, stands in the field with a handful of cut ears and an iron sickle. He tells her to cut only the heads, high on the stalk, and leave the straw standing for the cattle to graze.

lines.cy: Y pennau'n unig, cofia. Torra nhw'n uchel. Gad y gwellt yn sefyll i'r gwartheg.
lines.en: Heads only, mind. Cut them high. Leave the straw standing for the cattle.
lines.es: Solo las espigas, ojo. Cortalas arriba. Dejá la paja en pie para el ganado.

shots.direction: The harvest on the slope: the family cut the ear heads with small sickles and drop them into baskets while the wind runs through the standing grain.
Below them a boy drives the cattle up from the marsh with a hazel switch, the reeds swaying behind.
The mother watches him from the doorway and tells him the boy is bringing the cattle up off the marsh before the big tides come.

lines.cy: Mae'r bachgen yn dod â'r gwartheg lan o'r gors, cyn i'r llanw mawr ddod.
lines.en: The boy's bringing the cattle up off the marsh, before the big tides come.
lines.es: El muchacho está subiendo el ganado del bañado, antes de que lleguen las mareas grandes.

shots.direction: The elder, leaning on the wattle fence, answers quietly: last autumn the water came over the marsh in the night and they lost a calf.

lines.cy: Da iawn. Yr hydref diwethaf daeth y dŵr dros y gors yn y nos, a chollon ni lo.
lines.en: Good. Last autumn the water came over the marsh in the night, and we lost a calf.
lines.es: Bien. El otoño pasado el agua tapó el bañado de noche, y perdimos un ternero.

shots.direction: Inside, at the upright loom, she keeps weaving as she answers: not this year. The pig is fat, the store is full, and the cloth is nearly ready for the little one's cloak.

lines.cy: Nid eleni. Mae'r mochyn yn dew, mae'r stôr yn llawn, ac mae'r brethyn bron yn barod at glogyn y fechan.
lines.en: Not this year. The pig's fat, the store's full, and the cloth's nearly done for the little one's cloak.
lines.es: Este año no. El chancho está gordo, el granero lleno, y la tela casi lista para la capa de la más chica.

shots.direction: Dusk. A skein of geese crosses the sky over the marsh; the elder watches them go, smoke curling from the roundhouse.
He crouches beside his small granddaughter, points at the geese and tells her the cold is coming, and to bring wood in by the door tonight.

lines.cy: Gwranda, fach. Gwyddau'n mynd drosodd. Mae'r oerfel yn dod. Dere â choed at y drws heno.
lines.en: Listen, little one. Geese, going over. The cold's coming. Bring wood in by the door tonight.
lines.es: Escuchá, chiquita. Gansos que pasan. Viene el frío. Esta noche traé leña junto a la puerta.

shots.direction: Before dark the mother kneels at the spring below the homestead with a handful of the new corn: an offering to the water that has always kept them.

lines.cy: A chyn iddi nosi, mae llond llaw o'r ŷd newydd yn mynd lawr i'r ffynnon. Mae hi wastad wedi rhoi dŵr i ni.
lines.en: And before dark, a handful of the new corn goes down to the spring. It has always given us water.
lines.es: Y antes de que oscurezca, un puñado del grano nuevo baja al manantial. Siempre nos dio agua.

shots.direction: Time jump. Caption: c. AD 200, the same hill four hundred years on, a Romano-British farm at harvest. A late-summer field of spelt wheat, half reaped and stooked in rows, the river and marsh below; skylarks and wind.
captions: c. AD 200 · The same hill, four hundred years on

shots.direction: The farmer, bareheaded in a wool tunic and cloak with a bronze brooch, rubs an ear of spelt between his palms and talks to his wife: the fires are already lit up at the stone house over the brow, the spelt is good this year and dry enough to thresh before the rain comes up the valley.

lines.cy: Weli di'r mwg dros y grib? Ma' tân 'da nhw lan yn y tŷ cerrig yn barod. Sbelt da eleni. Digon sych i'w ddyrnu cyn i'r glaw ddod lan y cwm.
lines.en: See the smoke over the brow? They've the fires lit up at the stone house already. Good spelt this year. Dry enough to thresh before the rain comes up the valley.
lines.es: ¿Ves el humo sobre la cresta? Ya prendieron los fuegos allá arriba en la casa de piedra. Buen trigo espelta este año. Bastante seco para trillarlo antes de que la lluvia suba por el valle.

shots.direction: His wife keeps binding a sheaf beside a basket holding bread and a glossy red bowl. Then thresh it quick, she answers: the quern is hungry and so are the children; fine red pots from far off, and they still eat the same porridge out of them.

lines.cy: Dyrna fe'n glou, 'te. Ma'r freuan yn llwgu, a'r plant 'fyd. Potiau coch crand o bell, a ni'n dal i fyta'r un uwd mas ohonyn nhw.
lines.en: Then thresh it quick. The quern's hungry, and so are the children. Fine red pots from far off, and we still eat the same porridge out of them.
lines.es: Entonces trillalo rápido. La piedra de moler tiene hambre, y los chicos también. Ollas rojas finas de lejos, y seguimos comiendo la misma mazamorra en ellas.

shots.direction: The farmer swings his iron sickle through the spelt and lays the stalks down as she gathers and binds behind him.

She looks down the hill at grey cloud rising off the marsh and tells him to call the animals in. The geese are fat this year: one for the turn of the year, and one for his mother, or they will never hear the end of it.

lines.cy: Galw nhw miwn, 'te. Ma' cwmwl yn dod lan o'r gors. A ma'r gwyddau'n dew eleni: un at droad y flwyddyn, ac un i dy fam, neu chlywn ni byth diwedd y peth.
lines.en: Call them in, then. There's cloud coming up off the marsh. And the geese are fat this year: one for the turn of the year, and one for your mother, or we'll never hear the end of it.
lines.es: Llamalos, entonces. Viene una nube subiendo del bañado. Y los gansos están gordos este año: uno para el cambio de año, y otro para tu mamá, o no nos lo va a perdonar nunca.

shots.direction: He laughs and waves the geese off the sheaves: let them run, the hill is big enough for all of them.

lines.cy: Gad iddyn nhw redeg. Ma'r bryn yn ddigon mawr i bob un ohonon ni.
lines.en: Let them run. The hill's big enough for all of us.
lines.es: Dejalos correr. La loma es bastante grande para todos nosotros.

shots.direction: Rain cloud rolls in as the ox cart, loaded with sheaves, creaks up the earth track and the geese scatter beside it. End card: Cedwyn, Scene 2, The hill before the records. A tab.bot production.
End card: Cedwyn · Scene 2 · The hill before the records · A tab.bot production

en.intro: One unbroken scene on the same hilltop at Llandough, above the River Ely, in two moments four hundred years apart. First, about 200 BC: a late Iron Age family at their roundhouse bringing in the corn, minding the cattle on the marsh and preparing for winter. Then, about AD 200: a Romano-British farmer and his wife harvesting spelt on the same slope, with the stone house of the villa beyond the brow. Nobody speaks to the camera: they talk to each other, to a child, to the animals. They speak in modern Welsh, the nearest living language to their Brittonic, with English and Spanish subtitles. The faces are invented; no real person is shown.
